title: Aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING, Subqueries, and CTEs
learningObjectives: Explain how GROUP BY changes output grain.
Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and understand NULL behavior.
Choose between a subquery, CTE, and join based on clarity and semantics.
Avoid common aggregate errors caused by joins and ambiguous grouping.

mentalModel.text: Aggregation turns many rows into a summary. If a report should show one row per customer, GROUP BY customer_id defines that shape. WHERE decides which orders enter the calculation; HAVING decides which customer summaries stay in the final result. Decide what one output row means before writing the query.

concepts.title: GROUP BY defines the result grain

blocks.text: GROUP BY decides what one result row represents.

GROUP BY combines rows that share the same grouping values. Group orders by customer_id and the result has one row per customer with matching orders, not one row per order. Every other selected value must be calculated, grouped, or chosen with a clear rule.

blocks.title: Revenue per customer
blocks.source:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id;

blocks.title: Do not select arbitrary columns
blocks.content: A customer_id group can contain many orders. Selecting an order's created_at without defining which timestamp you mean is ambiguous. Aggregate it, group by it (which changes the grain), or use a window/latest-row pattern.

blocks.problem: The orders table has three orders for customer 7 and one for customer 9. You need total spend per customer.
reasoning: Group by customer_id and calculate SUM(total).
The result has one row for customer 7 and one for customer 9—not one row per order.
Selecting an order-specific timestamp without aggregating it or changing the grouping is ambiguous.
blocks.outcome: Before aggregating, say what one result row represents. That is the result grain.

blocks.text: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL. SUM and AVG also ignore NULL inputs.

COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(delivered_at) counts only rows where delivered_at is not NULL. SUM and AVG ignore NULL too. If there are no values to add, SUM returns NULL rather than zero. Use COALESCE only when zero matches the business meaning.

blocks.title: Count all rows versus known values
blocks.source:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS order_rows,
  COUNT(discount_amount) AS rows_with_discount_value,
  SUM(discount_amount) AS total_known_discount
FROM order_lines;

blocks.text: Use COALESCE only when replacing NULL with a specific value matches the business meaning. COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) may be appropriate for a report, but it collapses 'no known value' and zero into the same displayed result.

blocks.title: Empty input: SUM is NULL, not zero

blocks.text: An aggregate query without GROUP BY returns one row for empty input: COUNT(*) is 0, while SUM and AVG are NULL because there were no non-NULL inputs. A grouped query with no input rows produces no groups and therefore no rows. Use COALESCE only if zero is the correct business meaning.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL CTE behavior
blocks.content: PostgreSQL 12 and later can inline many eligible non-recursive CTEs. CTEs are not universally materialized; query shape and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED directives affect planning.

blocks.problem: Three delivery rows have delivered_at values of a timestamp, NULL, and NULL.
reasoning: COUNT(*) returns 3 because there are three rows.
COUNT(delivered_at) returns 1 because only one timestamp is present.
If SUM has no non-NULL values, PostgreSQL returns NULL; use COALESCE only if the report should treat that absence as zero.
blocks.outcome: Choose the aggregate based on what you mean to count. Missing data is not automatically the same as zero.

concepts.title: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups

blocks.text: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after the aggregate has been calculated.

blocks.title: Customers with more than five paid orders
blocks.source:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS paid_order_count
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

blocks.text: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after totals or counts are calculated. For example, use WHERE to keep paid orders, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 to keep customers with more than five paid orders.

blocks.title: HAVING is not a universal filter
blocks.content: Putting every filter in HAVING can force unnecessary grouping and make intent less clear. Use WHERE for row predicates and HAVING for group-level predicates.

blocks.problem: Find customers with more than five paid orders.
reasoning: Use WHERE status = 'paid' to remove unpaid orders before grouping.
Group the remaining rows by customer_id and count them.
Use HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 to keep only groups that meet the threshold.
blocks.outcome: Use WHERE for row-level conditions and HAVING for conditions on group totals or counts.

blocks.text: A subquery is a query inside another query. Its shape depends on whether you need one value, a set of rows, or just an existence check.

A subquery is a query inside another query. It can return one value, a set of rows, or test whether any row exists with EXISTS. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. None is automatically slow; first check correctness, then inspect the plan if performance matters.

blocks.title: Compare each order to its customer's average
blocks.source:
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
WHERE o.total_amount > (
  SELECT AVG(o2.total_amount)
  FROM orders o2
  WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
);

blocks.text: A correlated expression is logically evaluated with outer-row values, but PostgreSQL can choose an efficient plan. Check semantics first, then inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE if performance is in question.

blocks.problem: Find customers who have at least one paid order, without returning one row per order.
reasoning: A normal join can return the same customer multiple times when they have several paid orders.
EXISTS checks whether a matching paid order is present without adding child rows to the output.
A subquery is not automatically slower; check the plan if performance is in question.
blocks.outcome: Use EXISTS when the question is whether a matching row exists and you do not need the child data.

blocks.text: A CTE gives a meaningful query step a name, so a complicated query can be read as smaller stages.

blocks.content: In PostgreSQL 12 and later, many eligible non-recursive CTEs can be inlined into the surrounding query. A CTE is therefore not automatically a temporary table or a performance barrier. `MATERIALIZED` and `NOT MATERIALIZED` can influence the choice; check the plan before assuming either form is faster.
blocks.title: A CTE is a named query stage, not automatically a temporary table

blocks.text: A CTE is a named step in a query, introduced with WITH. It can make a report easier to read by naming an intermediate result, such as monthly revenue. PostgreSQL may combine that step into the larger query, so a CTE is not automatically a performance barrier.

blocks.title: Aggregate, then filter
blocks.source:
WITH customer_revenue AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, revenue
FROM customer_revenue
WHERE revenue >= 10000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

blocks.text: Use a CTE when naming a meaningful intermediate relation improves comprehension. Use a subquery when the expression is small. Use a join when combining related row sets is the clearest model. Validate performance from the actual plan rather than choosing syntax based on folklore.

blocks.problem: You need monthly paid revenue and want to show only months above $100,000.
reasoning: Use a CTE to calculate paid revenue grouped by month.
The outer query filters those monthly totals.
In PostgreSQL, a CTE is not automatically a performance barrier; inspect the plan if performance matters.
blocks.outcome: Use a CTE when naming an intermediate result makes logic easier to follow. Verify performance instead of assuming syntax determines it.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A report needs paid revenue per customer and only customers whose total exceeds ₹10,000. Filtering individual orders and filtering the final customer total are different operations.

2. Definition and design choice — GROUP BY creates one output row per group; aggregate functions summarize each group. WHERE filters input rows before grouping, while HAVING filters completed groups. CTEs and subqueries name stages but do not automatically make a query faster.

steps.title: Filter source rows
steps.description: WHERE removes rows that should not participate in the calculation.

steps.title: Form groups
steps.description: Rows sharing the grouping key belong to the same group.

steps.title: Compute aggregates
steps.description: SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, and MAX summarize each group; NULL handling differs by function.

steps.title: Filter grouped results
steps.description: HAVING tests aggregate results, then the query returns the remaining groups.

blocks.problem: Customer 7 has paid orders of ₹4,000, ₹3,000, and ₹5,000; customer 9 has ₹2,000. Return customers with paid revenue above ₹10,000.
reasoning: WHERE status = 'paid' decides which orders contribute. GROUP BY customer_id creates one result row per customer.
SUM(total_amount) gives customer 7 ₹12,000 and customer 9 ₹2,000; HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 10000 keeps only customer 7.
If another one-to-many table is joined before summing, repeated order rows can inflate revenue. Aggregate at the intended grain before combining independent child summaries.
blocks.outcome: Decide the output grain first, filter source rows with WHERE, and use HAVING for conditions on the aggregate result.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Do not select non-aggregated columns that are not functionally determined by the grouping key, or use HAVING for ordinary row filters when WHERE can reduce work earlier.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — You need total paid revenue per customer, but only for customers whose total exceeds ₹10,000. Where do the filters belong?
blocks.answer: Filter individual orders by paid status in WHERE, group by customer, compute SUM(amount), then use HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000.
blocks.explanation: WHERE controls input rows; HAVING controls groups. The distinction is both semantic and often relevant to efficiency.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: WHERE versus HAVING
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: WHERE reduces input rows; HAVING filters aggregated groups.

Failure mode: Row predicates are placed in HAVING, obscuring intent and potentially aggregating unnecessary data.

Decision rule: Filter individual records in WHERE; filter group metrics in HAVING.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column)
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values of that expression.

Failure mode: A nullable column is counted as if every row had a value, or a LEFT JOIN count includes the NULL-extended placeholder unexpectedly.

Decision rule: Choose the unit being counted explicitly. After an outer join, COUNT(child.primary_key) often counts real children while COUNT(*) counts result rows.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: COALESCE aggregate result to zero
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Zero can simplify reports; NULL may correctly mean no known value or no contributing rows.

Failure mode: A report hides the distinction between no data and a true zero.

Decision rule: Apply COALESCE at the boundary where the business contract defines how missing aggregates should be presented.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: CTE versus subquery
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: CTEs name logical stages; subqueries can keep small expressions local. PostgreSQL's planner may inline or materialize CTEs depending on query shape and directives.

Failure mode: A developer assumes WITH is always faster or always slower.

Decision rule: Prefer clarity, then inspect plans for materialization and performance effects on the actual PostgreSQL version.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Aggregation after one-to-many joins
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Joining before aggregation can provide needed dimensions but may multiply measures.

Failure mode: Revenue or counts are overstated by matching multiple child rows.

Decision rule: Define measure grain, inspect join cardinality, and aggregate independent relations before joining where appropriate.

revisionSheet.text:
What does GROUP BY define?

Answer: The grain of the result: one output row per distinct grouping-key combination after filtering.

WHERE versus HAVING?

Answer: WHERE filters input rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

COUNT(*) versus COUNT(x)?

Answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(x) counts rows where x is not NULL.

Do SUM and AVG count NULL as zero?

Answer: No. They ignore NULL inputs. Use COALESCE only when zero is the correct business meaning.

Does a grouped query return one row with zero when no rows match?

Answer: No. With GROUP BY, no input rows means no groups and therefore no output rows. An aggregate query without GROUP BY generally returns one row, with COUNT 0 and other aggregates often NULL.

Are CTEs always materialized in PostgreSQL?

Answer: No. PostgreSQL can fold eligible CTEs into the parent query; materialization depends on query shape, references and directives.

When should EXISTS be considered?

Answer: When the question is whether at least one related row exists and child values are not needed in the output.

What should you establish before aggregating?

Answer: The intended output grain and the unit represented by each measure.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters customers after their paid-order counts have been computed?

options.text: WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ON COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 5

questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups using aggregate results. WHERE filters rows before grouping.

questions.prompt: A table has 10 rows, and a nullable column x is NULL in 4 of them. What are COUNT(*) and COUNT(x)?

options.text: 10 and 6
6 and 10
10 and 10
6 and 6

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all ten rows; COUNT(x) counts the six non-NULL values.

questions.prompt: In modern PostgreSQL, every CTE is always materialized and prevents predicate pushdown.
questions.explanation: Eligible CTEs may be folded into the parent query. Actual behavior depends on query shape, references and materialization directives.

options.text: A GROUP BY query's output grain is determined by its grouping expressions.
COUNT(column) counts NULL values.
An outer join can make COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(child.id).
A subquery is always slower than a JOIN.

questions.explanation: Grouping expressions define output grain. NULL-extended rows can be counted by COUNT(*) but not by COUNT(child.id); optimizer transformations mean subqueries are not inherently slower.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE false;` return, and how can it return zero instead?

options.text: No rows; use GROUP BY to force a zero row.
NULL; use COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) if zero is intended.
0 because SUM treats empty input as zero.
An error because aggregates require a row.

questions.explanation: An aggregate query without GROUP BY returns one row for empty input, but SUM returns NULL. COALESCE can map it to zero when that is the intended business meaning.

questions.prompt: A report should return departments whose average salary exceeds 100000. Where should that aggregate condition go?

options.text: WHERE AVG(salary) > 100000
HAVING AVG(salary) > 100000 after GROUP BY department_id
ON AVG(salary) > 100000 without a join
ORDER BY AVG(salary) > 100000

questions.explanation: WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate values are calculated.

questions.prompt: Which statements about COUNT are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: COUNT(*) counts rows.
COUNT(column_name) excludes rows where that expression is NULL.
COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) counts distinct non-NULL values.
COUNT(column_name) always equals COUNT(*).

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL expression values; DISTINCT removes duplicate non-NULL values for the count.

questions.prompt: A CTE is always materialized and therefore always makes a query slower than an equivalent subquery.
questions.explanation: CTE optimization and materialization behavior depends on the database and query shape. In modern PostgreSQL, many non-recursive CTEs can be inlined; use EXPLAIN rather than assuming.

questions.prompt: You need customers whose total paid amount exceeds 5000, but only successful payments count. Which order of operations is most appropriate?

options.text: Group every payment, then filter individual rows with WHERE status = 'success' outside the aggregate
Filter successful payment rows, GROUP BY customer, then HAVING SUM(amount) > 5000
Use ORDER BY SUM(amount) before GROUP BY
Use DISTINCT amount to avoid aggregation

questions.explanation: Filter the input set to successful payments, aggregate by customer, then use HAVING to keep groups over the threshold.

questions.prompt: A query joins orders to items and payment attempts before summing order totals. Which changes can prevent inflated totals? Select all that apply.

options.text: Aggregate payment attempts to one row per order before joining.
Aggregate items to one row per order before joining if item-level columns are not needed.
Add DISTINCT to every selected column without analyzing the grain.
Document the intended row grain at each CTE boundary.

questions.explanation: Independent one-to-many relations can multiply each order. Pre-aggregation and explicit grain protect totals; arbitrary DISTINCT can hide rather than fix the bug.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid reason to use a CTE in a complex analytical query?

options.text: It guarantees a faster execution plan.
It makes logical stages explicit and can improve readability and reviewability.
It automatically adds indexes to intermediate results.
It makes NULL values behave like zero.

questions.explanation: CTEs can name and separate logical stages. They do not automatically guarantee speed, indexing, or different NULL semantics.

questions.prompt: WHERE is evaluated after HAVING, so WHERE can filter using aggregate results such as SUM(amount).
questions.explanation: WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate calculations.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Write a query to find customers whose total captured payments exceed ₹50,000, and explain how you avoid counting failed or duplicated payment rows.
strongAnswerPoints: State whether the measure is payment-level or order-level.
Group by customer identity and use HAVING for the aggregate threshold.
Check whether joins to line items or refunds could multiply payment rows.
Clarify currency, refund and reversal semantics.
pitfalls: Joining payment rows to multiple order lines before summing.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would first define the metric: captured payment amounts net of refunds, if that is what the business asks. I would filter to the qualifying payment states in WHERE, group by customer_id, sum at payment grain, and use HAVING SUM(...) > 50000. If other one-to-many tables are needed, I would aggregate them separately or use EXISTS to avoid multiplying payments. I would confirm currency and refund rules before presenting the result as revenue.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A monthly revenue report returns inflated totals after a developer joins orders, order_items, and payment_attempts. Refactor the query conceptually and explain how you would validate the result.
strongAnswerPoints: State the required output grain, such as one row per month and currency.
Decide whether revenue means order value, captured payment value, or net revenue after refunds.
Aggregate items and payment attempts separately to the needed grain before joining.
Filter qualifying rows before aggregation and use HAVING for aggregate thresholds.
Handle NULL/no-row aggregates deliberately rather than assuming zero.
Validate against hand-calculated fixtures with multiple items and multiple payment attempts per order.
pitfalls: Assuming a CTE automatically improves performance.
Using SUM(DISTINCT amount) as a universal de-duplication strategy.
Combining currencies or refunds without defining the metric.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: First I would define revenue precisely and state the report grain, including month and currency. The raw joins multiply rows because one order can have multiple items and payment attempts. I would aggregate each source independently, for example payment attempts to one row per order and items to one row per order, then join those aggregates and group to month. Filters on raw rows belong before aggregation; thresholds on aggregate results belong in HAVING. I would test orders with multiple items, retries, partial captures, refunds, and no qualifying payments against hand-calculated expected totals. Finally I would inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE for performance rather than assuming the CTE shape is faster.

description: Aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING, Subqueries, and CTEs. Interview-focused explanations, worked examples, trade-offs, and practice.
